stages.sub: What the central bank does for government and banks, and why it regulates the industry.

steps.q: The government needs to borrow £50 billion this year by selling bonds, and needs somewhere to hold its day-to-day cash. Which institution handles this for it?
steps.hint: Think about which single institution oversees the whole monetary and banking system.

steps.q: A commercial bank suddenly cannot get enough cash to meet withdrawals and no other bank will lend to it. Who can step in to lend to that bank when nobody else will?
steps.hint: Just as the government has one bank to rely on, so do commercial banks.
steps.pre: Being the bank that commercial banks can turn to, and lending when no one else will, makes the central bank

steps.q: If a bank's managers know that the central bank will always rescue them from a cash crisis, how carefully will they weigh up risky lending decisions?
steps.right: Less carefully, since a rescue is expected
steps.hint: Recall moral hazard: when someone is protected from the consequences of their choices, how do their choices change?
steps.pre: So the promise of rescue itself encourages excessive risk-taking, which is the

steps.q: Beyond lending, the central bank also sets rules banks must follow, checks their capital levels, and can fine or restrict banks that break the rules. What kind of role is this?
steps.right: Overseeing and controlling the banking industry
steps.hint: Think about who is checking that banks behave properly, not just lending to them.

steps.q: A lender cannot fully tell how risky a borrower really is before lending to them. Should rules exist requiring borrowers to disclose more information?
steps.right: Yes, to reduce this information gap
steps.wrong: No, lenders should just guess as before
steps.hint: Recall the problem where one side of a deal knows more than the other.

steps.q: Traders at several banks secretly agree to fix an interest rate benchmark used across the whole economy, distorting prices for everyone. Should this kind of behaviour be controlled by rules?
steps.right: Yes, rules are needed to stop it
steps.wrong: No, the market will correct it itself
steps.hint: This is deliberate manipulation of a market price, not an honest mistake.

steps.q: One bank collapsing can cause savers to panic and pull money from other banks too, even healthy ones, dragging down the whole financial system. Does this spillover cost only affect the bank that failed?
steps.right: No, it spreads costs across the whole system
steps.wrong: Yes, it stays contained to that one bank
steps.hint: Think about how the failure of one firm can impose costs on people and firms outside that failure.
